academicJudgment.claim: A broader UCR programme in economics, public finance and policy meaningfully responds to the confirmed economic-effects and fiscal-policy inquiry, while supplying substantially less statutory-tax and advanced-accounting specialisation.
academicJudgment.basis: All six taught economics courses now sustain economic models, policy effects, behavioural decisions and causal/predictive inquiry. Public Economics directly teaches taxation and redistribution; Microeconomics supplies labour/capital/externality/incentive analysis and Macro fiscal policy. Accounting/finance/legal-institutional teaching provides specific business context. The actual external public-finance module and economic-effects programme questions support this limited broader response.
academicJudgment.strongestObjection: Fiscal Economics requires advanced tax/reporting and interpreting fiscal law; a generic business/economics curriculum cannot be relabelled fiscal training. Those known requirements remain prominent unmatched gaps. The approved claim is a broader economic/public-finance response, sustained beyond one tax paragraph by multiple actual economic/methodological courses and specific legal/accounting context. This moderate academic judgement differs from CP396 only after independent target/content review, not because its name includes Economics.

contributions: Actual legal foundations, institutions, justice and public/private law supply legal context for economic regulation, without teaching fiscal legislation.
Actual firm organisation, stakeholders, business decisions and value creation provide business context for economic effects on firms; no tax-planning sequence.
Actual micro/macro models, incentives, strategic interaction and market/aggregate analysis provide substantive foundations for fiscal-policy questions.

Actual international legal sources, responsibility and institutions provide a bounded legal framework; no tax treaties or international tax doctrine are inferred.
Actual constitutional/public institutions and administrative principles support government/regulation inquiry; not Dutch fiscal procedure.
International-relations theories, institutions and country-position research provide specific context for cross-border political/economic decisions, not international tax law.
Actual rights, dignity, equality and legal/philosophical argument add normative criteria for fairness questions; no specialised taxpayer-rights doctrine.
Description-only: actual psychological deviations, biases, framing and experiments extend economic decision analysis; tax-compliance experiments are not promised.
Actual macroeconomic models, growth, expectations, fiscal/monetary policy and open economies provide substantive fiscal-policy/economic-effects analysis.

Actual financial statements, management accounting, budgets, costs and discounted investment appraisal supply accounting/firm substance. One course does not reproduce three financial-reporting stages, advanced tax accounting or taxable-profit computation.
Actual EU institutions, competences, free movement and enforcement supply EU legal foundations, not state-aid/direct-tax analysis as a specialised fiscal sequence.

Actual labour/capital markets, market power, externalities and government intervention give economic tools for analysing fiscal incidence/incentives. Detailed tax-law applications are not asserted as taught.

Actual public goods, efficiency/equity, expenditure, health/welfare/social insurance, taxation and redistribution directly sustain public-finance inquiry. This goes beyond generic economic coherence, but does not reproduce Dutch tax-base/rate doctrine.
Description-only: policy-making phases, alternative conceptualisations and policy memos through a sugar case support policy analysis; the case is not automatically a taught tax experiment.

Actual property/tort/contract doctrine and comparative IRAC/case research, including France/Germany/England/China/US, provide substantive private-law context for business decisions. No fiscal statute or Dutch tax computation is inferred.
Actual European decision rules, actors and policy-document inquiry supply political/institutional context for cross-border fiscal-policy questions.
Actual international business strategy, institutional governance and ethics support analysis of multinational business decisions; not international tax structures/treaty planning.
Actual data cleaning, transformation, visualisation and exploratory questions supply concrete empirical workflow; a tax dataset or project is not guaranteed.
Description-only: OLS/GLS/instrumental variables, inference, Monte Carlo work and an empirical paper sustain economic causal/predictive inquiry. No fiscal dissertation equivalence.
Actual asset valuation, risk, banking regulation and financial instruments supply finance and investment context; not complete advanced corporate finance or tax accounting.
Actual qualitative design, interviews, coding/reflexivity and a team inquiry supply qualitative empirical methods; no fiscal interview project is guaranteed.
Actual consequentialist/Kantian/virtue/feminist theories and close argumentative reading supply substantive ethical judgement for fairness questions without being a specialised fiscal-ethics course.
